title: Find the second-largest element without sorting (track top two in one pass).
shortTitle: Find the Second-Largest Element Without Sorting
keyPoints: Track two variables: largest and secondLargest, updating both in a single pass through the array.
When a new element beats the largest, demote the old largest to secondLargest before updating largest.
The ordering of the demotion is critical: copy largest to secondLargest before overwriting largest.
Decide deliberately whether duplicates of the maximum count as the second largest or not.
Guard edge cases: arrays with fewer than two elements or all identical values have no distinct second largest.
Time is O(n) and space is O(1), far better than sorting at O(n log n).

s1_definition.oneliner: Keep a gold and a silver tracker; a new champion pushes gold down to silver, otherwise it may just claim silver.
s1_definition.profdef:
- **Two trackers** – maintain `largest` and `secondLargest` variables in a single pass.
- **Demotion rule** – when a new element beats the largest, the old largest becomes the second largest.
- **Runner-up check** – if the element is between the two trackers, update only secondLargest.
- **O(n) time, O(1) space** – one pass, two variables, far cheaper than sorting.
- **Duplicate policy** – decide whether to require the second largest to be strictly less than the largest.
s1_definition.analogy: The risk team at National Bank of India wants the second-highest transaction on Priya's account this month, because the top transaction is often a known salary credit and the second-highest is the one they actually scrutinise. Instead of ranking every transaction, a clerk walks the list holding a gold medal and a silver medal. When a bigger amount appears, the current gold holder is demoted to silver and the newcomer takes gold.

sections.s6_takeaway:
Finding the second-largest element without sorting is a single pass that tracks the top two values. I keep a largest and a second-largest, and for each element I apply an ordered check: if the element beats the largest, I first move the current largest down into the second-largest and then make the element the new largest; otherwise, if it sits strictly between the two, I update the second-largest.

The detail that trips most people up is the ordering inside the first branch. I must copy the old largest into the second-largest before I overwrite the largest, otherwise I lose the value that should become the runner-up. I also decide deliberately how to treat duplicates: for a distinct second-largest I require the candidate to be strictly less than the largest.

In my banking project at National Bank of India, I used this on the risk team's monthly scan of Priya's account, where the highest transaction is usually a predictable large credit, so it is the second-highest distinct amount that actually gets scrutinised.

Remember one sentence: demote the current largest to second-largest before crowning the new champion, and always handle the all-identical edge case.
